The Mississippi Legislature concluded its 2026 session with several major immigration-related measures enacted that strengthen cooperation between state and local officials and federal authorities. FAIR actively shaped several of these bills, offering policy input, drafting statements of support, and mobilizing grassroots activism.

One of the most significant measures this year was Senate Bill 2114, which establishes new state penalties related to illegal immigration and expands cooperation with federal enforcement. The law makes it a felony for an alien to enter or attempt to enter Mississippi directly from a foreign nation at a location other than a lawful port of entry. It also directs the Mississippi Department of Public Safety to identify illegal aliens within the state and requires the department to work with federal authorities. In addition, the legislation requires county detention facilities to participate in the federal 287(g) program, allowing local authorities to act as a force multiplier helping to carry out certain immigration enforcement functions.

Lawmakers also approved House Bill 538, another major enforcement measure that strengthens Mississippi’s existing prohibition on sanctuary policies. The bill expands the state’s anti-sanctuary statute to include any policy or practice that limits or interferes with the enforcement of federal immigration law. Additionally, it requires state and local government entities and employees to cooperate with federal authorities when enforcing immigration laws and authorizes the attorney general to investigate and prosecute violations.

A third enforcement measure advanced during the session was Senate Bill 2322. The bill addresses issues related to state identification and driver’s license policies, including provisions addressing the validity of certain out-of-state licenses issued to individuals unable to prove lawful presence in the United States.

In addition to FAIR sending statements of support to Mississippi leadership, we encouraged activists to urge lawmakers to pass SB 2114, SB 2322, and HB 538, recognizing the bills as some of the strongest enforcement proposals considered during the session. By aligning state enforcement authority more closely with federal law, the measures ensure that individuals who enter the country unlawfully and commit crimes in Mississippi can be identified and removed.

The Legislature also enacted Senate Bill 2588, which includes provisions addressing identification requirements tied to immigration status, and requires the verification of an applicant’s citizenship upon receipt of a completed voter registration application. While not as sweeping as some of the other immigration measures debated this year, the bill represents another step taken by Mississippi lawmakers as part of a broader effort to address immigration-related policy concerns at the state level.

The 2026 legislative session marked a significant step forward for immigration enforcement policy in Mississippi. With multiple bills enacted into law strengthening cooperation with federal authorities and reinforcing the state’s opposition to sanctuary-style policies, lawmakers signaled a clear commitment to prioritizing public safety and the rule of law.

Kansas recently enacted strong immigration enforcement legislation when lawmakers successfully overrode Governor Laura Kelly’s veto of Kansas House Bill (HB) 2372.

HB 2372 establishes new procedures governing how local law enforcement agencies in Kansas interact with federal immigration authorities. Among its key provisions, the law authorizes county sheriffs to honor federal immigration detainer requests and clarifies the standards under which individuals may be held in local custody pursuant to those requests. The legislation also provides legal protections for law enforcement officers who cooperate with federal immigration enforcement actions and outlines procedures for notifying individuals who are subject to immigration detainers.

Perhaps most significantly, the measure allows Kansas law enforcement agencies to enter into cooperative agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement under the federal 287(g) program without first obtaining approval from local governing bodies such as county commissions.

Under 287(g) agreements, state and local officers can receive federal training and authority to assist with certain immigration enforcement functions, typically within local detention facilities. These agreements can help ensure that individuals who are subject to immigration enforcement are identified while already in local custody, allowing federal authorities to assume custody in a controlled detention setting rather than attempting to locate those individuals later in the community.

The bill moved through the Kansas Legislature earlier this year as lawmakers debated the role of state and local agencies in federal immigration enforcement. After the legislation passed both chambers, it was vetoed by the governor. Supporters in the legislature responded by initiating the formal veto override process, ultimately securing the votes necessary in both the House and Senate to enact the measure into law despite the veto.

Advocates of stronger immigration enforcement had followed the bill closely throughout the legislative process. FAIR activists also acted during the legislative process contacting lawmakers, urging the bill’s passage, and encouraging support for the veto override.

With legislation now enacted, Kansas joins a number of states that have taken steps in recent years to expand cooperation between state and local law enforcement agencies and federal immigration authorities. Such cooperation can help ensure that individuals who are subject to federal immigration enforcement actions are properly identified and transferred to federal custody.

May 2025 | A FAIR Research Report

Executive Summary

Sanctuary jurisdictions—states and localities that obstruct federal immigration enforcement—pose a serious threat to the safety and security of the American people. What began as an effort to reassure “law-abiding” illegal aliens that they could safely report crimes or assist law enforcement without fear of deportation has evolved into a scheme that protects illegal aliens, even violent criminals, from being turned over to federal immigration authorities.

The number of sanctuary jurisdictions has surged over the years, increasing from fewer than a dozen in the 1990s to 564 in 2018.[1] According to FAIR’s latest tally, as of May 2025, at least 1,003 sanctuary jurisdictions in the United States shield illegal aliens from immigration enforcement, openly undermining the rule of law.

Of the total number of sanctuary jurisdictions, 17 states and Washington, D.C. have state-wide sanctuary policies. There has also been an alarming trend of some localities strengthening their pre-existing restrictions on cooperating with the federal government. Fortunately, other state and local governments are proactively adopting laws that require more cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. However, despite the fact that 23 states have banned sanctuary policies, some local jurisdictions still defy these state laws. Only four states with anti-sanctuary laws—Arkansas, Montana, West Virginia, and Wyoming—are entirely free of sanctuary jurisdictions.

Thus, states with anti-sanctuary laws must do more to enforce these policies. States like Indiana serve as a model for what can be accomplished when there is the political will.

Background

Sanctuary jurisdictions have been around since at least the 1980s. However, their expansion across the country is a relatively recent—and increasingly troubling— phenomenon. What started as a small movement has since been expanded by open-border advocates, resulting in a widespread trend that undermines federal immigration law and threatens national security.

Sanctuary jurisdictions, as defined by FAIR, are states or localities that have enacted laws, ordinances, policies, practices, resolutions, or regulations that prohibit or impede communication or cooperation with immigration officials, or otherwise obstruct the enforcement of U.S. immigration laws.

Contrary to what open-border proponents may argue, sanctuary policies conflict with federal law. Most importantly, they contradict Article I, Section 8, Clause 4 of the Constitution, which gives Congress plenary authority over immigration; Article VI of the Constitution, which, through the Supremacy Clause, provides that federal law takes precedent over conflicting state laws; and Article II of the Constitution, which, through the Take Care Clause, vests within the Presidency the authority—and indeed, the duty—to ensure the laws are faithfully executed.[2], [3], [4]

Sanctuary policies also violate federal statutes. While sanctuary laws vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, they generally violate 8 U.S.C. § 1373, which prohibits state and local governments from restricting the sharing of immigration information with federal immigration authorities; 8 U.S.C. § 1324, which prohibits the harboring of illegal aliens; and 18 U.S.C. § 1501 et seq., which criminalize the obstruction of justice.[5], [6], [7]

Sanctuary cities also contradict federal policy, which clearly envisions state and local cooperation, and certainly not resistance, in enforcing federal laws. Congress expressly authorized immigration agencies to issue detainers to state and local law enforcement agencies under 8 U.S.C. § 1226 and 8 U.S.C. § 1357 (without a judicial warrant).[8] Additionally, pursuant to 8 U.S.C. § 1357, no formal agreement is required for any state or local employee to communicate with federal immigration officials regarding the immigration status of any individual or to otherwise cooperate in the “identification, apprehension, detention, or removal of aliens not lawfully present in the United States.”[9]

In this report, a state or local government qualifies as a sanctuary jurisdiction if it obstructs the enforcement of federal immigration law. Examples of obstruction include:

Prohibiting law enforcement officers or public employees from cooperating with federal immigration authorities;

Prohibiting law enforcement officers from honoring an ICE detainer or directing officers to ignore ICE detainers;

Prohibiting law enforcement officers or other public officials from inquiring about immigration status or sharing such information with federal officials;

Denying federal immigration officers access to jails, prisons, or courthouses;

Requiring a “judicial” or “court-ordered” warrant to comply with a detainer request;

Enacting policies that prohibit the construction of immigration detention centers or prohibit state or local jurisdictions from entering into contracts with private detention facilities;

Restricting prosecutors or court officials from sharing information related to an alien’s court proceedings; and

Allowing aliens to plead to lesser charges or a lesser sentence to avoid immigration consequences.

According to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a detainer is a request “that asks a federal, state or local law enforcement agency—including jails, prisons or other confinement facilities—to:

Notify the requesting agency as early as possible before they release a removable alien.

Hold the alien for up to 48 hours beyond the time they would ordinarily release them so DHS has time to assume custody in accordance with federal immigration law.”[10]

Many state and local jurisdictions refuse to honor detainers issued by ICE because they claim that “judicial” or “court-ordered” warrants are required for prisons or jails to hold aliens already in their custody. However, sections 236 and 287 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. §§ 1226 and 1357) authorize federal immigration agencies to issue detainers without a judicial warrant.[11] The truth is, states and local subdivisions that require judicial warrants intend to impose restrictions on federal immigration agents above what is required in federal law because they want to obstruct immigration enforcement and overwhelm the judicial system.

Current Trends

FAIR has vigilantly monitored the expansion of sanctuary cities, thoroughly reviewing state and local policies that obstruct federal immigration enforcement. Our findings reveal that, prior to 2000, only 11 jurisdictions had adopted sanctuary policies. By 2009, that number had grown to 40.[12] In 2016, it had surged to over 300, and by 2018, FAIR identified 564 jurisdictions as noncooperative.[13], [14] Now, the number of sanctuary jurisdictions stands at 1,003.

Since the presidential election in November 2024, many sanctuary jurisdictions have doubled down on their policies. For example, the City of Los Angeles, which previously relied on informal policies, has now enacted formal ordinances that shield illegal aliens from removal proceedings.[15] In Pima County, Arizona, the sheriff’s department was previously the only agency operating under sanctuary guidelines. However, as of January 2025, the entire county has been directed to follow sanctuary policies.[16] In Berkeley, California, the mayor publicly pledged to reaffirm the city’s longstanding sanctuary status in response to President Trump’s immigration policies.[17] The Berkeley City Council obliged.[18] In Providence, Rhode Island, the mayor’s office has expressed similar intentions.[19] And in Austin, Texas, both the mayor and the police chief have pledged their continued support for the city’s sanctuary policies.[20], [21] Across the nation, jurisdictions continue to disregard federal immigration law and, in doing so, place the safety of the American public at risk.

Entire states have institutionalized sanctuary practices as well. Currently, 17 states and the District of Columbia have statewide sanctuary laws, policies, or legal opinions in place. These include California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Utah, Vermont, Washington, and Washington, D.C. Some states, like Nevada, are de facto sanctuary states, due to their intimidating and coercive tactics, using “model-immigration policies” that pressure jurisdictions to conform to sanctuary practices. Although Nevada’s state-wide “model” policy does not explicitly ban cooperation with federal immigration authorities, jurisdictions must justify their decision to opt out. As a result, the state meets FAIR’s criteria for classification as a sanctuary state.

Many states have expanded their sanctuary policies over time. For example, Washington state now requires all schools to adopt policies consistent with statewide sanctuary guidelines and schools in Vermont are instructed to deny entry to federal immigration authorities unless presented with a “judicial” warrant.[22], [23] Additionally, the governors of Massachusetts and Oregon have affirmed that their states will uphold sanctuary policies despite federal opposition.[24], [25]

In contrast, 23 states have banned sanctuary policies, encouraging or even requiring local law enforcement officers and other officials to cooperate with federal immigration officials. Those states, also referred to as anti-sanctuary states, are Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, New Hampshire (effective in 2026), North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, West Virginia, and Wyoming.

Unfortunately, while these states have enacted anti-sanctuary laws, only some states have taken the critical step of enforcing them. Three states, Arkansas, Montana, and West Virginia, have succeeded in eradicating sanctuary jurisdictions within their borders. But local jurisdictions in some anti-sanctuary states, such as Georgia, Iowa, and North Carolina, continue to defy state laws. States must do more to ensure that their anti-sanctuary laws are enforced to protect public safety and uphold the rule of law.

While Indiana has not yet completely eliminated its sanctuary cities, it serves as a blueprint for other states to follow. Indiana adopted a statewide ban on sanctuary policies that could not be enforced because of a court decision. In order to ensure that the state’s anti-sanctuary law had teeth, the legislature provided an enforcement mechanism, which gave the state’s Attorney General standing to sue local jurisdictions to enforce state law. With that power, State Attorney General Rokita worked with FAIR to identify multiple municipalities that had enacted sanctuary policies that violated state law. He then issued those jurisdictions warnings to rescind their sanctuary policies, indicating that if they didn’t, he would sue. Some jurisdictions corrected course, and the Attorney General sued the jurisdictions that did not. Other governors should take note: laws without enforcement are meaningless and actions to fight noncompliance are effective.

Some states have faced ongoing legal battles that place the status of their anti-sanctuary laws in flux. Texas is a prime example. In 2017, Governor Abbott signed Senate Bill (SB) 4 into law, which aimed to ban sanctuary jurisdictions and mandate cooperation with federal immigration authorities.[26] The law immediately faced legal challenges, resulting in parts of it being temporarily blocked before a federal appeals court ultimately upheld most provisions, allowing the law to be enforced.

Florida has gone through similar challenges. In 2019, the state passed SB 168, which banned sanctuary policies and required local law enforcement to cooperate with federal immigration authorities.[27] That law was challenged, and, in 2023, a three-judge panel for the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals overturned the ruling that blocked parts of the law. The same year as the 11th Circuit’s decision on SB 168, Florida lawmakers worked to expand anti-sanctuary law with the introduction of SB 1718, which prohibits sheltering or transporting illegal aliens within the state.[28] While SB 1718 was signed into law, certain provisions have since been temporarily halted by the courts. These cases highlight how even states that enact strong anti-sanctuary laws often face a legal tug-of-war, resulting in patchwork enforcement.

Sources and Methodology: Focus on Practices, Not Labels

This report is based on a variety of sources, including primary documents such as laws, resolutions, ordinances, and policy directives. This report also used secondary sources like the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s Declined Detainer Outcome Report, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Detainer Acceptance Tracker, academic studies, records requests, direct quotes from public officials, and media coverage.

Oftentimes, a municipality will adopt a label such as “Welcoming,” “Inclusive,” or “Safe Haven.” These jurisdictions may not officially identify as sanctuary jurisdictions, and may even reject the term altogether. However, while such labels alone do not qualify a locality as a sanctuary jurisdiction, the adoption of policies that restrict communication or cooperation with immigration officials does. In conclusion, their actions convey more than the labels assigned to their policies. In rare instances, self-identified sanctuary jurisdictions are excluded if they cannot be verified as actually adhering to sanctuary policies.

WASHINGTON—The Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) has filed a brief in the U.S. Supreme Court urging the Court to review a decision in a set of consolidated lawsuits against an Arizona law requiring state election officials to verify the U.S. citizenship of those applying to vote in federal elections in the state. A federal district court has struck down the law as preempted under the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed that decision.

Under a federal law, states have to “accept and use” a particular federal-government voter registration form when signing up people to vote in federal elections. In an earlier case, the Supreme Court struck down an earlier Arizona law that required applicants using that form to provide proof of citizenship with the form. The Court held that Arizona was not “accepting and using” the federal form —which only had a citizenship check-box, and did not require proof of citizenship—because it added to its requirements.

As FAIR points out in its brief, the current Arizona law accepts the federal form as-is. Then, however, election officials are supposed to verify citizenship claims on the form by looking at databases. If they are not able to verify an applicant’s citizenship, even after contacting the applicant and asking for proof, they cannot register the applicant to vote.

The Constitution puts the states, not the federal government, in charge of voter qualifications (such as citizenship) in federal elections. And the citizenship requirement Arizona seeks to verify is vital to the right of the American people to govern themselves. Arizona’s power to set voter qualifications is meaningless if it cannot police its most important qualification, citizenship.

“No federal law can require states just to presume that people who say they are U.S. citizens are telling the truth, and the Supreme Court never said otherwise,” said Dale L. Wilcox, executive director and general counsel of FAIR. “We hope the Court takes this case to overrule the Ninth Circuit and uphold this obviously-constitutional, necessary law.”

The cases are Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota, No. 25-1017, Warren Petersen v. Mi Familia Vota, No. 25-1019, and Arizona v. Promise Arizona, No. 25-1022 (Supreme Court).

The Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment provides that those “born … in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof,” are U.S. citizens. U.S. Const. Amend. XIV, § 1. The Clause was adopted to confer citizenship on the newly freed slaves and their children, not on the children of aliens temporarily visiting the United States or of illegal aliens . On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order No. 14,160, Protecting the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship, which restores the original meaning of the Citizenship Clause and provides, on a prospective basis only, that children of temporary visitors and illegal aliens are not U.S. citizens by birth. The Citizenship Order directs federal agencies not to issue or accept citizenship documents for such children born more than 30 days after the Order’s effective date.

The question before the U.S. Supreme Court is whether the Executive Order complies with the Citizenship Clause and with 8 U.S.C. 1401(a), which codifies that Clause .

The Supreme Court has long read the Clause to mean that a person becomes a citizen by birth only if he is “completely subject” to the United States’ “political jurisdiction”— that is, only if he owes “direct and immediate allegiance” to the United States and may claim its protection. In United States v. Wong Kim Ark, the Supreme Court clearly held that, to be subject to the jurisdiction of the United States at birth, and thus a citizen under the Fourteenth Amendment, one must be born in the United States to parents who are permitted by the United States to reside here . The Court also listed some exceptions, including “children of diplomats, children of invading armies, and children of tribal members.”

The lower court enjoined President Trump’s Executive Order, finding that “subject to the jurisdiction thereof” refers to all babies born on U.S. soil, aside from the enumerated exceptions in Wong Kim Ark.

FAIR filed a brief in the U.S. Supreme Court showing that by limiting citizenship to children born to parents who are permitted by the United States to reside here, Wong Kim Ark largely resolves the question presented in this case . Illegal aliens and temporary visitors are not permitted to reside here, so their children are not citizens under the Fourteenth Amendment.

FAIR also showed that the lower court’s interpretation that children of illegal aliens are citizens should be disfavored because it forces citizenship on the nation . The American concept of citizenship requires mutual consent between the nation and the individual, but under Plaintiffs’ view, not only are the children of illegal aliens citizens despite the lack of consent to their citizenship by the political branches, they are citizens even though the political branches have prohibited the necessary condition for their citizenship, the presence of their parents. On Plaintiffs’ view, the citizenship of this class of individuals is forced upon the nation against its political will . Given the centrality of mutual consent in the American idea of citizenship—and also because a citizen of the United States is no mere subject, but shares in the sovereignty of the people over this country, see U.S. CONST. Preamble—this interpretation is to be disfavored.

Oral argument was held on April 1, 2026, and the Court’s decision is expected by June .

The agencies that protect our borders are housed within the Department of Homeland Security. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is the main agency responsible for securing our borders. CBP includes the U.S. Border Patrol, the Office of Field Operations and Air and Marine Operations. The Border Patrol is responsible for patrolling territory between[2] official ports of entry and 2,000 miles of coastline surrounding the Florida Peninsula and the island of Puerto Rico. The Office of Field Operations is responsible for guarding 328 official ports of entry[3] to the United States. Ports of entry may be located along our land borders or maritime borders (i.e., seaports). Other ports of entry are located in the interior of the U.S. – namely at international airports, such as JFK airport in New York City.

Border Security may be measured in several ways. One important measure of border security is the number of aliens who are caught illegally entering the United States. Pre-COVID, the agencies categorized this number in two ways. The Border Patrol would report on the number of illegal aliens “apprehended”, and the Office of Field Operations would report on the number of “inadmissible” aliens who showed up at the ports of entry. Despite the two terms, both represent the same thing: aliens who have crossed into the U.S. illegally. Then in 2020, with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic and the implementation of the Title 42 expulsion authority, the agencies began to group apprehensions, inadmissibles, and Title 42 expulsions (which technically were not “apprehensions” or “inadmissbles” because they were not conducted under the authority of Title 8) under the umbrella term “encounters.”[4]

Another important measure of border security is how many illegal aliens have crossed the border but were able to evade capture. These are typically called “gotaways.” While it may seem counter-intuitive, Customs and Border Protection regularly calculates the number of gotaways (even if it does not publish the information). It does so by logging the number of aliens agents witness crossing into the U.S. and are unable to capture for various reasons (such as distance or insufficient agents or vehicles on hand). Drone footage or radar may also supply CBP with additional numbers of gotaways.

Border security may also be measured by the arrests of alien smugglers, the quantity of illegal drugs seized, the number of vehicle incursions along the border, and other violence at the border such as assaults on U.S. border agents. The exploding fentanyl crisis, for example, has demonstrated how Mexican drug cartels have exploited weaknesses in recent border policies that dedicate border agents to processing and releasing illegal aliens instead of patrolling the borders. Cartels then use the absence of agents as an opportunity to bring in fentanyl and other drugs without resistance.

Finally, border security may be measured by our effectiveness in screening aliens who enter the U.S., legally and illegally. For example, the number of suspected terrorists apprehended illegally entering the U.S. between the ports of entry has grown from 2 in FY 2017 to 172 in FY 2023.

Government agencies typically report border security statistics by month and fiscal year. For the federal government, the fiscal year (FY) runs from October of one year through September of the following year. For example, Fiscal Year 2023 began on October 1, 2022, and ended September 30, 2023.

Terminology

To better understand this essay, and other work published by FAIR, several commonly used terms should be defined. An alien, as defined by federal law, is any person who is not a citizen or national of the United States. An illegal alien is simply any alien who is present in the United States without legal status. In addition, while certain illegal aliens may be described as “lawfully present,” this is not the same as having legal status. For example, recipients of deferred action, deferred enforced departure, Temporary Protected Status (TPS), or parole are generally considered lawfully present, but they do not have legal status and thus they are still illegal aliens. Rather, the government has merely deferred their deportation for a period of time, and that deferral has led to them being described as “lawfully present.” Thus, when eligibility for a benefit, such as Obamacare or a driver’s license, is described as available to aliens who are “lawfully present,” this generally means both illegal aliens who are lawfully present and legal aliens may apply.

In addition, those who cross the border illegally and claim asylum are illegal aliens, even though the law permits them to request asylum pursuant to various restrictions and regulations. Some advocates have described seeking asylum as “lawful immigration.” While this may be true for aliens who come to the U.S. on visas and claim asylum, this is not true for illegal border crossers. An alien who enters illegally is still an illegal alien, whether or not he or she applies for asylum. Aliens who cross illegally and claim asylum remain illegal aliens until their case is adjudicated, which could be years down the road. Nevertheless, the law allows them to apply for work eligibility and other benefits despite the fact that they have no legal status.

This Earth Day, let’s take a moment to explore a critical, but often overlooked, threat to the environment: mass immigration. Texas has been a popular destination for millions of immigrants, legal and illegal, as well as hundreds of thousands of Americans seeking more opportunity. A direct outcome of this swift growth is urban sprawl in all directions across the state, irreversibly destroying Texas’s natural landscape. Two areas are suffering the brunt of this destruction: Greater Houston and Dallas-Fort Worth.

Just northeast of Houston sits Colony Ridge, a 40,000-acre “colonia” that is home to tens of thousands of illegal aliens and is an alleged cartel hub for drug smuggling and sex trafficking. FAIR has covered many of the spillover effects of this community on the surrounding area. One of the biggest victims is the local environment. Where once stood large swaths of East Texas’s Piney Woods, a valuable ecoregion, now sits a poorly designed development known as the “largest trailer park in the country.”

These numbers are very worrying because Colony Ridge was four times smaller than its current size when the study was carried out. If something isn’t done to slow the growth of this poorly designed “colonia,” Houston could be one bad rainstorm away from its water supply being contaminated.

Rapid urbanization and population growth are also having a devastating effect on the environment of North Central Texas. North Central Texas contains the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex, which has an estimated 8.3 million residents, and the region’s population has grown by nearly 900,000 since 2020, driven by high immigration levels. To accommodate this steady decades-long growth, cities have had to sprawl out in all directions, resulting in the destruction of Texas’s famed prairies. Once occupying an area of 12 million acres that stretched from San Antonio to north of Dallas, only about 5,000 acres of the Blackland Prairie remain. Prairies are essential for ecological balance as they mitigate droughts, limit flood risks, and replenish groundwater. A report on Texas prairies from the World Resources Institute explains that one acre of tall grass can hold and clean up to 250,000 gallons of rainfall, which would play a major role in alleviating water demand. Inside Dallas itself, the destruction of its remaining prairies is leading to the extinction of several native wildlife species and threatening dozens of others. Additionally, the risks of flooding and the “urban heat island effect” are ever-increasing.

The Lone Star State is one of the crown jewels of the United States. It’s time that this runaway population growth and urban sprawl are put under control, and that Texas realizes its true strength lies in the diversity of its animal life and plant life.

History

Congress, in 1929, created a provision in law to include a “registry” allowing illegally present aliens in the United States to obtain lawful permanent residence (LPR) if they entered the country before a specific date. This cutoff date, which originally applied to those who entered before June 3, 1921, required that aliens demonstrate good moral character and continuously reside in the U.S. since they entered. That cutoff date was updated several times. Today, the registry is effectively obsolete as the date has been fixed at 1972 since Congress last amended the statute in 1986.

In 1986, Congress granted amnesty to three million illegal aliens through the passage of the Immigration Reform and Control Act (IRCA), allowing them to obtain lawful permanent residence status. That bill, also known as the Simpson-Mazzoli Act, was signed into law by President Reagan on November 6, 1986. It opened a door that politicians since then have failed to close. This legalization massively incentivized more illegal immigration and sent a message to illegal aliens that the law would not be enforced and one day, they, too, could benefit from amnesty if they waited.

The 1986 law was authored to be a 3-legged stool – control of illegal immigration, a legalization program, and reform of legal immigration. The committee report accompanying IRCA stated, “the solution lies in legalizing the status of aliens who have been present in the United States for several years, recognizing that past failures to enforce the immigration laws have allowed them to enter and to settle here.” When President Reagan signed IRCA into law, he stated that the legislation was a major step toward meeting the challenge to our sovereignty while at the same time preserving and enhancing the nation’s heritage of legal immigration.

In 2000, Congress again passed legislation to allow certain illegal aliens to qualify for LPR status, regardless of how one entered or if they were working without authorization. This time, Congress adopted the Legal Immigration Family Equity (LIFE) Act and LIFE Act Amendments of 2000, which established section 245(i) within the INA. Certain aliens were eligible to apply for green cards by filing a form and paying a $1,000 fee.

In 1996, Congress amended the INA to create “cancellation of removal.” Cancellation of removal allows unlawfully present aliens who have been in the U.S. for at least ten years to avoid deportation by claiming hardship. During immigration proceedings, aliens may seek amnesty through cancellation of removal if they can establish “exceptional and extremely unusual” hardship to family members.

FAIR shows administration’s action is unreviewable

WASHINGTON—The Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) has filed a brief in the U.S. Supreme Court urging the Court to reverse lower court orders blocking the Trump Administration’s termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for citizens of Haiti and Syria. Under the TPS statute, the Secretary of Homeland Security may determine whether persons from a given country, because of disastrous conditions in their homeland, may live in the United States for a set period of time, and may renew this status for further such periods if conditions warrant.

Trump’s Secretary of Homeland Security, Kristi Noem, obeying an executive order by the President, determined that TPS for both Haiti and Syria was no longer appropriate under the TPS statute, and terminated those statuses. Two federal district courts, finding that these decisions violated the Administrative Procedure Act, issued orders blocking the Secretary’s termination decisions. The U.S. Courts of Appeals for the Second Circuit and District of Columbia Circuit both declined to stay the lower courts’ judgments.

In its brief supporting reversal of these orders, FAIR demonstrates that, according to longstanding Supreme Court precedent, the President, as Commander-in-Chief, has inherent authority to protect the nation by excluding aliens. That means Secretary Noem’s actions pursuant to Trump’s order were presidential actions. Presidential actions are immune from review under the Administrative Procedure Act. FAIR also shows that the TPS statute expressly strips courts of jurisdiction to hear this case, by barring judicial review of “any determination … with respect to [a] designation” of TPS. The determinations Noem arrived at in terminating these TPS designations were certainly “with respect to” such a designation.

“The President is not a federal agency, and is not subject to the Administrative Procedure Act,” said Christopher J. Hajec, deputy general counsel of FAIR. “And it was the President who acted here, through his executive order. We hope the Court does not ignore the President’s constitutional power over foreign affairs, sees that the courts lack jurisdiction over this case on multiple grounds, and reverses.”

The cases are Mullin v. Dahlia Doe, No. 1083, and Trump v. Miot, No. 1084 (Supreme Court).

Data from other countries in the Americas show Chinese nationals are prepared to use circuitous routes to reach the U.S. This is problematic because it can lead to the increased influence of Chinese criminal organizations in Latin America and their cooperation with the cartels.

Chinese nationals have high rates of filing asylum claims, and large-scale asylum fraud is an “open secret” amongst Chinese migrants. Since most Chinese nationals are economic migrants, they seek to be released in order to obtain employment.

China’s government policies support the manufacture and distribution of fentanyl in the U.S., which kills tens of thousands of Americans every year.

Mexican cartels have formed an alliance with China to flood the U.S. with drugs, giving cartels power to control the border and incentive to traffic foreign nationals over the border.

Chinese nationals, both illegal aliens and those legally present, have been implicated in espionage on a massive scale. China costs the U.S. economy hundreds of billions of dollars a year through theft, much of which is facilitated by legal and illegal immigrants.

Section 1: Background

China’s authoritarian government is the top adversary of the United States, and its ruling Chinese Communist Party (CCP) wishes to see America weakened and replaced as a global hegemon. As Michael Pillsbury, a leading China expert, emphasized, “[t]he hard truth is that China’s leaders see America as an enemy in a global struggle they plan on winning.”[1] This perception was reinforced over the past decade under Xi Jinping, who has been the leader of China since 2012.[2] Indeed, the 2024 Annual Threat Assessment of the U.S. Intelligence Community, written by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, highlights China before any other global threat, detailing how China wishes to undermine the U.S. and place itself as the global leader.[3] Against this backdrop of hostility and rivalry, the skyrocketing levels of illegal migration from communist China under the Biden administration are just another example of the serious threats China poses to our national security.

Prior to the Biden administration taking office, encounters of Chinese illegal aliens at our borders were at relatively low levels. For example, in FY19, there were only 6,100 border encounters. However, in FY21, a total of 23,471 Chinese nationals were encountered, with the numbers rising every subsequent fiscal year. During the first ten months of FY24, 67,665 Chinese nationals were encountered, almost triple the number of FY21 encounters. These numbers do not include “gotaways,” i.e., those who evaded law enforcement but were seen entering by Border Patrol, which reached historic and alarming proportions under the previous administration. During a congressional hearing in May 2024, Simon Hankinson, an expert on border security at The Heritage Foundation, warned that the sheer numbers of unvetted migrants had the potential to allow criminals and other threat actors to enter the U.S.[4]

The surge in border encounters since 2021 has serious national and community safety implications. According to Craig Singleton, senior director of the China program at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies, weak border security could allow operatives from China to gain entry to the U.S. for nefarious purposes.[5] China has even used the chaos at the U.S. border in its propaganda, portraying the U.S. as a declining power unable to secure its borders and therefore unworthy of global respect.[6]

As subsequent sections will lay out, the harm caused by mass migration can have serious consequences. These range from espionage, crime, and drug and human smuggling to collaboration with brutal Mexican drug cartels to import deadly fentanyl – all of which harm American security and national interests.

Section 2: Data on Border Encounters and Demographics

Increase in Encounters (2012-2024)

Illegal immigration from China was historically low relative to China’s massive population. For most of the period before 2019, the number of Chinese nationals encountered by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) was relatively modest. From 2012, the year Chinese leader Xi Jinping came to power, to 2019, the last year before the COVID-19 pandemic, encounters of Chinese nationals averaged just 5,200 per year.[7] Chinese nationals accounted for as few as 0.5 percent of encounters of all nationalities in the years 2012 to 2019.

This situation has been changing rapidly as enormous numbers of Chinese nationals entered the U.S. since 2020. In FY20, 18,395 Chinese were encountered by CBP at America’s borders.[8] In FY21, this number grew to 23,471 encounters and grew again in FY22 to 27,756 encounters.[9]

From FY22 to FY23, the number of encounters with Chinese nationals more than doubled to 52,700.[10] FY24 saw the highest number of illegal crossings from Chinese nationals ever recorded, reaching a shocking 78,701.[11] In total, during the Biden administration, over 200,000 Chinese nationals were encountered by CBP.

Push or Pull? The Real Factors Driving the Numbers

Both push and pull factors play a role in illegal immigration. The former are associated with factors driving people out of a country, like a poor economy or political conflict, and the latter are attractive factors like open-borders policies in the destination country.[12] It may be tempting to see the sudden surge in Chinese migration as being motivated by a desire to flee an oppressive regime, but this contention falls flat when examining the evidence. In terms of push factors, China’s trend of particularly strong repression began well before 2020, but its economic struggles coincide with both the COVID-19 pandemic and the surge in illegal immigration. The key factor in spurring the wave of illegal immigration was the pull of the Biden administration’s open borders on that struggling population.

China has been a totalitarian communist state since the CCP took power in 1949 and has consistently ranked as one of the worst countries in the world for human rights and personal freedoms.[13] Despite decades of oppression since, there was historically no great exodus towards the U.S. China did at one point restrict emigration through an exit permit regime, like the former Soviet Union, but during and after those restrictions individuals leaving China went mostly to Hong Kong and other nearby countries.[14] Before 2020, relatively few Chinese were encountered by CBP, suggesting the political repression was not enough to motivate Chinese would-be illegal aliens to cross the Pacific.

The sudden and massive uptick in encounters of Chinese nationals by CBP has occurred at a time when China’s government is dealing with massive economic, not political, turmoil. The economic downturn in China since COVID-19 coincides with increases in Chinese border encounters and is strongly suggestive of economic motivations driving at least some of the recent Chinese migration. This would undercut claims by migrants claiming to be seeking asylum, when the real motive is often economic.[15] The heretofore strong (on paper) Chinese economy was badly hit by COVID-19, and its recovery has been relatively slow.[16] In a U.S. House hearing before the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, Commissioner James Mann stated “Beijing’s Zero-COVID policy has caused significant damage to China’s economy,” and China investment expert Shehzad Qazi told the hearing China’s COVID lockdowns had “devastated every segment of China’s economy.”[17] This has been particularly difficult for young Chinese.[18] As shown by the case of Venezuela, however, economic struggles alone do not spur illegal immigration to the U.S. without policies that allow that migration in.[19]

The main reason for the sudden uptick in Chinese nationals was not the push factors in China — political or economic — but rather the pull factors generated by the former Biden administration. The Biden administration essentially operated a “catch-and-release” policy on the border letting virtually anyone, from anywhere, enter and remain in the U.S. All that prospective illegal aliens had to do was make it to the U.S. border. Asylum applicants, even economic migrants with frivolous applications, could receive an employment authorization document (EAD) and Social Security number.[20] All that was required was that a migrant made it to the border, and this resulted in a profusion of routes being used to reach it.

Section 3: The Changing Landscape of Chinese Entry Routes

Making it to America’s border is not an easy process for would-be illegal aliens from China, making the Biden-era large increase in Chinese nationals worthy of deeper examination. Unlike other origin countries of illegal aliens, China is geographically distant from the U.S. border. Furthermore, the Chinese passport is considered “weak”, and the U.S. requires Chinese nationals to obtain a visa in advance of arrival. Citizens of China have visa-free access to just 85 countries and territories as of 2025, compared to American passport holders who have visa-free access to 186 countries.[21] Few of the visa-free destinations the Chinese can enter are physically near the United States. Because of this situation, Chinese nationals without the means or ability to get a U.S. visa will “shop around” the few nations that offer visa-free access, aiming for a country as close to the U.S. itself as possible, then making the rest of the journey to the U.S. border by other means.

Would-be illegal aliens have two main pathways through the Americas to the U.S. border: entering a country in Latin America and then making their way from there to the U.S.-Mexico border or going directly to Mexico from China using a legitimate visa for Mexican entry and then heading to the U.S. border.

Ecuador: Chinese Migrants Entering but Not Going Home

Ecuador is the most prominent example of how a country’s loose visa policies allow illegal migrants from China to reach the U.S. border. The South American nation is notable for only requiring visas for travelers from a small list of nations, meaning even holders of “weak” passports can obtain entry to the Americas visa-free through Ecuador.[22] From 2016, China was included in that visa-free group with the expectation that it would be a viable trading partner. Initially, the deal worked as intended. FAIR looked at Ecuadorian government data on entries and exits by Chinese nationals. In 2021, Ecuadorian immigration data recorded a modest 5,568 Chinese nationals entering the country, and 5,551 of them (99 percent) were recorded flying back to China.[23] However, this began to change dramatically as the Biden administration’s policies took full effect.

In the first full year of the Biden administration, Chinese nationals entering Ecuador dramatically increased, but revealingly, the number returning to China dropped. In 2022, the number of Chinese entering Ecuador increased by 146 percent to 13,705, with some 2,700 (nearly 20 percent) not returning to China.[24] In 2023, as the situation at the U.S. border was spiraling far out of control and China’s economy was clearly slowing, Ecuador’s position as a stepping stone for Chinese illegal immigration was cemented. A record 48,381 Chinese nationals entered Ecuador in 2023, and 24,141 (nearly half) did not return to China.[25] Entries of Chinese migrants headed for the U.S. border became so common that a cottage industry sprang up in Ecuador that caters to Chinese-speaking travelers headed to the U.S. border.[26]

The data on Chinese overstays in Ecuador align closely with data on Chinese nationals in countries that lie further along the route to the U.S. border. Is it possible the Chinese nationals really did return to China, but the government of Ecuador simply failed to track it? Maybe so, but data on Chinese nationals in other countries along the route between Ecuador and the U.S., such as Panama and Mexico, line up very closely with the number of Chinese nationals who failed to leave Ecuador under the terms of their tourist visa. This is very strong statistical evidence to suggest Chinese nationals were taking advantage of this route to reach the U.S.-Mexico border.

In June 2024, Ecuador suspended visa-free entry for Chinese nationals, explicitly referencing abuse of the system by Chinese migrants as the reason. However, this only occurred after tens of thousands of illegal migrants had already taken advantage of the route it created.[27] Ecuador’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated the government had noted “unusual increase in irregular migratory flows of Chinese citizens” and expressed its suspicions that these migrants were using Ecuador as a stepping-stone to “other destinations in the hemisphere.”[28]

Ecuador’s recent changes to visa requirements will only affect one part of the vast network through which Chinese illegal migrants come to the U.S. border. Some reporting suggests that visa-free Bolivia may become the starting point of an even longer overland route, stretching 7,000 miles from that country’s capital, La Paz, to the U.S. border.[29] Given what we have seen in other parts of the Americas, it seems like a possible developing route Chinese illegal aliens will exploit.

Panama: Darién Gap Data Show Vast Increase in Chinese Nationals

The surge in Chinese migration generated by weak border security in the U.S. under the Biden administration was felt across the Americas, and Panama was no exception. The Darién Gap on the Panama-Colombia border was once renowned as a quiet and underdeveloped region, with people urged to stay away.[30] Since 2021, this once relatively tranquil region had become a thoroughfare for over 1 million migrants, and the U.S. largely failed in its efforts to slow the flood (until the Trump administration returned to power).[31] While the vast majority of illegal crossers through the Darién were from South America or the Caribbean, a sharp increase in Chinese migrants was also clearly visible in available data.

FAIR looked at Panamanian data on migrants in the Darién Gap and noticed an alarming increase in numbers coinciding almost perfectly with the Biden administration’s term in office. Throughout the 2010s, illegal Chinese migration through the Darién Gap was extraordinarily low. Just 296 Chinese nationals crossed through in that entire decade, with 2010 alone accounting for 90 percent of that figure. Without the pull of an open U.S. border, coupled with bullish economic conditions in China, attempting the dangerous trek was a hard sell for most nationalities, including Chinese. Weak U.S. border policies drew Chinese migrants north from Ecuador and elsewhere. Just over 2,000 Chinese migrants came through the Darién Gap in 2022, up from nearly zero throughout the prior decade. Interestingly, this is the same year that 2,700 Chinese nationals flew into Ecuador but did not return to China.[32]

By 2023, Chinese nationals became the fourth most common nationality of migrants in the Darién Gap. In 2023, a record 25,565 Chinese made the trip through Darién, again closely mirroring the Ecuadorian data of over 24,000 Chinese entries.[33] As in Ecuador, businesses catering to Chinese migrants have built up in and around Panama, with buses and guides charging migrants around $9,000 to $12,000 each.[34] Occasional arrests of smugglers have not dampened the appetite for these services.[35]

The Chinese-owned and CCP-linked social media app TikTok has been used by Chinese migrants to facilitate their journeys through the Darién Gap in Panama to the U.S. border. This has come to the attention of the U.S. House Committee on the Budget.[36] The hashtag #darien had been viewed 1.6 billion times by October 2023. These circuitous routes to the U.S. border via Ecuador and Panama are less desirable than a more direct route via Mexico. Would-be illegal aliens with the means (or assistance from the Chinese government) can take advantage of tourist visa rules in Mexico and bypass most of the long trek to the border through the rest of Latin America to begin with.

Mexico: The Door to the U.S. for Illegal Aliens

While many Chinese nationals have entered the U.S. via a long journey through the Americas, some are able to fly direct from China to Mexico. The long journey via Ecuador through the rest of the Americas is long and undesirable, costly and dangerous. Mexico is ideal as it is directly next to the border the Chinese ultimately want to cross. The Chinese middle class, the dominant background of Chinese migrants “are not rich enough to use education or work opportunities as a means of entry [to the U.S.], but they can afford to fly across the world.”[37]

During the Biden administration, Chinese nationals were encountered in vastly increasing numbers making their way to the U.S. via Mexico, and Mexican data confirm this. The Mexican government publishes the Boletin Mensual de Estadisticas Migratiorias, which catalogs illegal migrants detected by Mexican authorities by nationality and other factors. The number of Chinese illegal migrants encountered by Mexican authorities was exceptionally low in the decade before the Biden administration took office, with fewer than 100 individuals in 2014 and as few as 14 in 2018.[38] 1,200 Chinese illegal migrants were detected in Mexico in 2022, and this number surged to a record total of over 14,000 in 2023.[39]

While Mexico requires a visa for Chinese nationals to enter legally, a loophole exists that can be exploited.[40] For instance, the visa requirement is waived if the Chinese national already holds permanent residency in the U.K., Japan, the Schengen Area or the Pacific Alliance countries (Chile, Colombia, Mexico, and Peru).[41] Just holding a permanent visa for any of those countries except Pacific Alliance members also grants visa-free entry. This means Chinese nationals could obtain legitimate visas from more than 30 different third countries, use these visas to enter Mexico, and then make their way north to the U.S. border and enter illegally.

In addition to this visa loophole, some Chinese take advantage of the fact that certain flight routes to Mexico are less likely to be subject to controls and checks than others. For Chinese nationals in a position to pay $20,000, smugglers will help Chinese migrants obtain Japanese tourist visas and transport them to the U.S. border once they’ve flown into Mexico on those visas.[42] The “agencies” arranging this travel will attempt to place Chinese migrants on flights where authorities are least likely to stop them, leading to connections through third countries.[43]

Section 4: Asylum

It is tempting, but inaccurate, to claim that most Chinese nationals’ motivation for coming to the U.S. illegally is to seek asylum from the CCP. Bona fide political asylum cases did not drive the exponential increase in encounters. China did not suddenly become a repressive state in 2021, when the number of Chinese illegal aliens surged. However, it has suffered serious economic disruption and a deflationary crisis in that period.[44]

The U.S. is clearly the preferred destination of most Chinese “asylum seekers,” who are in many cases truly economic migrants. The United Nations estimates that 137,143 Chinese nationals lived abroad as asylum seekers by the end of 2023, with the vast majority of them (112,495) in the U.S.[45] Once Chinese migrants make it past the U.S. border, either by being allowed in or by paying tens of thousands of dollars to be smuggled in, they have the option of applying for asylum as a route to gain legal status.[46] Economic reasons are not valid grounds for asylum, so many Chinese nationals solicit the help of lawyers who coach them with fake stories of political or religious oppression.[47]

Illegal migrants entering the U.S. have two options when they apply for asylum. They can file an asylum application directly with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) on their own behalf (“affirmative asylum”). If they are given a notice to appear in immigration court, they can also file for asylum in that court as a defense against being deported (“defensive asylum”). This takes place through the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR). Despite many having purely economic motivation for seeking asylum and often making fraudulent claims when applying, data show that Chinese nationals are more likely to be granted asylum than most other nationalities seeking asylum in the U.S.

Chinese nationals were granted asylum in 3,481 defensive asylum cases in FY23, the most grants of any nationality and had an overall grant rate of 55 percent.[48] This compares to an overall grant rate of just 28.3 percent for defensive asylum cases in that fiscal year, and lower than 10 percent for other numerous groups like Salvadorans, Hondurans, and Guatemalans.[49] Affirmative asylum grants to Chinese nationals were down to 1,538 in FY22 from nearly 4,000 in FY19 but this drop corresponds with an overall decline in cases adjudicated by USCIS.[50] With better chances of approval than most other nationalities, Chinese nationals have strong incentives to apply for asylum as soon as they have the opportunity. As of 2024, there is a backlog of over 73,000 asylum cases involving Chinese nationals.[51]

In the event that an immigration judge denies the asylum request, the judge would then issue a final order of removal. However, in such cases, it is nearly impossible for the U.S. to deport Chinese nationals because their home country generally refuses to accept them. China has long been identified as one of the major “recalcitrant countries” which consistently block the deportation of their own nationals by refusing to issue travel documents or otherwise not accepting their return.[52] Deportations to China have to be specially arranged on charter flights at great expense to the U.S. government, and are rare enough that a single flight can make national headlines.[53] Case law generally prevents the U.S. government from holding illegal aliens that it cannot deport in custody for more than six months, so Chinese nationals can remain free indefinitely even if their asylum requests are rejected.[54]

Internal data obtained by the New York Times in 2023 showed that 100,000 Chinese nationals living in the U.S. have final orders of removal, meaning that theoretically they should be deported immediately.[55] However, with fewer than 300 people deported to China from the U.S. in all of FY23, Chinese migrants are confident they will not face consequences if they enter illegally, no matter the ultimate result of their asylum case.[56] Many of them freely admit that their motives are economic (which is never grounds for asylum), with some able to achieve “monthly earnings now exceeding $10,000” as they wait for immigration court cases far in the future.[57] It remains to be seen whether the Trump administration’s renewed focus on recalcitrant countries can make a dent in this backlog.[58]

No matter how illegal aliens from China address their status, they can benefit from the same informal networks that helped most of them arrive in the first place. Immigration court case data, a proxy for illegal entries, show massive influxes of Chinese nationals into the traditional gateways of Los Angeles and New York City.[59] From there, illegal aliens from China can meet with long-established networks catering to new migrants that can place them in under-the-table jobs and informal housing across the country as they work off debt to smugglers.[60]

Chinese communities in the U.S. are ready-made networks for illegal aliens from China, giving them the ability to disappear and seek informal jobs and housing.[61] This means that Chinese illegal aliens are rarely long-term users of the shelter systems that have devastated the finances and public safety of local jurisdictions, especially “sanctuary cities.” However, other social problems caused by the fact that some Chinese migrants work for organized crime can occur.

Section 5: Drugs and Crime

A weak border and weakly enforced immigration laws provide fertile conditions for foreign criminal actors to operate. Open borders allow people to be smuggled more easily by smugglers and traffickers, and overworked Border Patrol agents processing migrants (instead of being on the line) are less able to interdict drug smuggling.[62] But arguably the most dangerous type of criminality linked to Chinese criminal actors (and even the Chinese government) is the role Chinese actors play in the fentanyl trade.

One of the most immediate and pressing dangers of an unsecured border is the flooding of our communities with illicit and dangerous drugs. The deadliest drug currently being smuggled into the U.S. is fentanyl, and communist China is crucial in its manufacture, export and distribution. Fentanyl – whose street names include “China Girl” and “China Town” – is an extremely potent synthetic opioid that is 50 times stronger than heroin and 100 times stronger than morphine. A dose as small as 2mg – the equivalent of 5-7 grains of salt – is sufficient to kill one person.[63] In 2023, an estimated 74,702 Americans died from synthetic opioid overdoses, with fentanyl being the most prominent type.[64] Since 2020, around half of all U.S. drug deaths have been linked to synthetic opioids. Thus, it’s more suitable to say fentanyl is a poison, rather than suggesting these deaths are caused by an overdose.

The Chinese Government Actively Supports Drug Smuggling into the U.S.

China is the number one origin of chemicals that make fentanyl, and the Chinese government actively encourages and enables the deadly criminal enterprise through generous policy interventions. The House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party emphasized this fact in a lengthy and detailed report it produced on the CCP and the fentanyl crisis. The report states, “[t]he PRC, under the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), is the ultimate geographic source of the fentanyl crisis. Companies in China produce nearly all of illicit fentanyl precursors, the key ingredients that drive the global illicit fentanyl trade.”[65] These include directly subsidizing the manufacturing of fentanyl chemicals, providing tax rebates to companies producing them, and giving monetary grants and awards to companies that openly traffic fentanyl precursors.[66]

The CCP’s support for fentanyl has been described as part of an explicit geopolitical strategy. On March 23, 2023, a House of Representatives Subcommittee on National Security, Illicit Finance, and International Financial Institutions heard testimony that China was using drug smuggling to weaken the U.S. and its people.[67] The Chinese military also produced a treatise on effective tactics in asymmetrical warfare, which includes “drug warfare that cause[s] disasters in other countries and make[s] huge profits” as one such tactic, which is clearly being employed against American society now.[68]

According to the Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, the CCP plays a role in the fentanyl crisis in the following ways: The PRC Government fails to prosecute fentanyl precursors and synthetic narcotics manufacturers

The PRC Government has thwarted U.S. law enforcement investigations into illicit fentanyl manufacturers

The PRC allows the open sale of fentanyl precursors and other materials that fuel the fentanyl crisis on the extensively surveilled Chinese internet

The PRC government censors content about domestic drug sales—but leaves export-focused narcotics content untouched

The PRC aggressively prosecutes domestic drug trafficking but leaves illicit drug exports untouched

The Chinese government, running a totalitarian state with intensive mass surveillance, is in a position to stop fentanyl trafficking if it wished, but does not do so. The CCP tightly regulates the internet in China yet allows “the open sale of fentanyl precursors and other illicit materials on the extensively monitored and controlled PRC internet.”[70] As China expert Vanda Felbab-Brown pointed out, China’s “operational law enforcement cooperation tends to be highly selective, self-serving, limited, and subordinated to its geopolitical interests.” Felbab-Brown continued: “Chinese criminal groups cultivate political capital with Chinese authorities and government officials abroad by also promoting China’s political, strategic, and economic interests.”[71]

Also of interest is the relationship between the CCP and Chinese criminal gangs. Former Attorney General William Barr testified in front of the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party in April 2024. He detailed how China works with criminal actors to produce illicit drugs and provide financing and laundering to criminal actors. He told Congress, “The CCP has been tightening its alliance with Chinese organized crime to gain influence outside of China, and U.S. law enforcement investigating Chinese money laundering have found evidence indicating that some schemes involve Chinese Government officials and Communist Party elites.”[72]

The China-Mexican Cartel Alliance

The nexus between the Chinese communist regime, Chinese organized crime, and Mexican cartels is a fact, and the danger posed by this unholy alliance is encouraged and amplified by open-borders policies. As part of this process, fentanyl precursor chemicals are shipped from communist China to Mexico, where the powerful drug cartels, mainly the Sinaloa Cartel and Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG), synthesize them in labs to produce finished fentanyl, or mix it into other drugs and pills, and attempt to traffic it into the U.S. to poison Americans.[73]

The weak policies pursued by the Mexican government have provided almost perfect operational conditions for the China-Cartel alliance to operate. The administration of former Mexican president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador (known as AMLO), who served from 2018-2024, was very permissive towards cartel activity. AMLO disbanded anti-cartel units in the police, urged the U.S. not to launch anti-cartel activity and did not share data on drug seizures with the U.S. government.[74] These policies allowed the CCP-allied cartels to operate with much greater freedom and impunity.

In addition to fentanyl production, Chinese gangs have been running marijuana growing operations that have violated various legal requirements even in states where marijuana is now legal. In August 2023, a memo leaked from Border Patrol showed that illegal marijuana farms make Chinese criminal gangs over $4 billion annually.[75] One law enforcement source, speaking on the condition of anonymity to the press, said that gangs use Chinese nationals who have ongoing asylum claims to work for them, as it is harder to deport them.[76] Multiple U.S. states, both at the border and the interior, have been impacted.

In the summer of 2023, New Mexico law enforcement raided facilities where Chinese nationals were employed. As one media outlet described, they were part “of a new pipeline of migrants leaving China and making unauthorized border crossings into the United States via Mexico, and many are taking jobs at hundreds of cannabis farms springing up across the U.S.”[77] Other border states like California have also been impacted. In 2022 in Newberry Springs, California, a Chinese gang was charged with illegal marijuana distribution and environmental law breaking after a 14,000 square foot facility for drug production was discovered.[78]

Even America’s smallest towns, some thousands of miles from the border, have not been spared these marijuana operations run by Chinese gangs.[79] In Maine, for example, small communities with populations of barely a few thousand inhabitants have been targeted by Chinese marijuana operations. A leaked unclassified memo from DHS reportedly showed over 100 properties in Maine linked to Chinese marijuana gangs.[80] This situation is undercutting legal marijuana businesses in the state.[81] The situation prompted a U.S. Senator from Maine to write a letter to the DOJ urging a crackdown on CCP-linked marijuana operations in the state.[82]

In addition to drug smuggling, the smuggling of women and children has also flourished thanks to the cooperation between China and the cartels. Many times, the two activities increasingly go hand in hand and cannot be viewed as two distinct criminal operations, part of a model dubbed “poly-crime” by experts.[83] At the U.S.-Mexico border itself, according to cartel expert Robert Almonte, Chinese poly-crime organizations are collaborating with Mexican cartels in migrant smuggling by “paying the Mexican cartel some kind of a percentage, quota or tax.”[84]

Chinese criminal actors have been implicated in the sexual exploitation of women and girls who come to the U.S. illegally from China. Criminals recruit poor women in rural parts of China, promising them good jobs in the U.S., and then force them into prostitution in massage parlors once they arrive in the U.S.[85] In 2022, nine men were federally charged with 31 counts for running a prostitution ring that exploited female Chinese illegal aliens.[86] The gang was accused of shuttling women across multiple states for sex, and ruthlessly beating any women who resisted.[87]

Building a case against their abusers is tricky. Dominique Roe-Sepowitz, Director of the Office of Sex Trafficking Intervention Research (STIR) at Arizona State University, notes that some abuse victims “…may be too ashamed to leave and accept help, when it is normal in their culture to keep abuse a secret.”[88] A roundtable discussion at the Congressional Executive Commission on China heard testimony that some women from China feel a sense of familial obligation to accept sex work to support the family, complicating efforts to investigate it as it clashes with cultural notions of duty and filial obligation.[89] Periodic raids that break up brothels disguised as massage parlors only have a short-term impact.[90]

Section 6: National Security

China Exploits Our Open Borders and Generous Visa Policy

Weak border security compounds the danger that China poses to U.S. national security. The FBI publicly considers the policies pursued by China’s authoritarian government to be “the greatest long-term threat to our nation’s information and intellectual property, and to our economic vitality.”[91] This threat is compounded by a 2017 Chinese law explicitly requiring Chinese citizens, in the country or abroad, to cooperate with government intelligence-gathering activities.[92] The Chinese government exploits the American immigration system in a number of ways to further its goals, clearly linking immigration to the largest national security issue America faces today.

The situation regarding China’s exploitation of America’s weak borders has alarmed lawmakers. In June 2023, 11 Members of Congress on the U.S. House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party co-signed a letter to then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin and then-FBI Director Christopher Wray expressing alarm at Chinese espionage.[93] In September 2023, five U.S. Senators sent a letter asking former Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas to clarify what security measures were in place in response to increased Chinese activity at the U.S. border.[94] Most recently, in June 2024, James Comer, Chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability, wrote a 13-page letter to then-Secretary Mayorkas detailing China’s abuse of the U.S. immigration laws.[95]

Key points of the Comer letter “Using a form of warfare meant to corrode the United States from within, the CCP has infiltrated U.S. critical infrastructure, bolstered the illicit drug trade globally, engaged in unlawful and exploitative immigration by infiltrating our borders (…).”

“Notably, some Chinese illegal immigrants ‘have been found to have links’ with the CCP and the PLA, and reportedly, ‘border chiefs are concerned more could be slipping through their grasp.’ DHS has been remiss in confronting the surge in Chinese nationals entering the United States via Mexico.”

“[S]ome Chinese nationals are brought to America and forced to work on marijuana-growing operations in which Chinese transnational criminal organizations are heavily involved.”

The CCP actively seeks to insert itself into Chinese diaspora communities to surveil and persecute dissidents, influence our political system, and otherwise work on behalf of Beijing’s hostile objectives.

One of the most widespread and brazen examples of Chinese exploitation of the American immigration system is the “gate-crasher” phenomenon. WHO IS AN ILLEGAL ALIEN?

An illegal alien is simply any alien who is present in the United States without legal status, like a valid visa or lawful permanent residence.

It is important to note that “legal status” is not the same as “lawful presence.” For example, recipients of deferred action, deferred enforced departure, Temporary Protected Status (TPS), or parole do not have legal status. These programs (some of which are authorized by statute and some are not) do not give illegal aliens visas or green cards. They merely defer deportation for a period of time.

Nevertheless, these aliens are still described as “lawfully present” or as having “lawful presence.” That is because “lawful presence” is a term of art under immigration law designed to clarify that although an alien has no legal status, he or she is not accruing unlawful presence for purposes of the three and ten-year bars under Section 212(a)(9) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA).[3]

Pursuant to Section 212(a)(9), an alien who has no legal status will start to accrue days of unlawful presence. If the alien accrues more than 180 days of unlawful presence and is then deported or otherwise leaves, the alien is barred from admission for three years. If the alien accrues 365 or more days (one year) of unlawful presence and is then deported or otherwise leaves, s/he is barred from admission for ten years.[4]

However, if an alien is granted a deferral of deportation, such as deferred action, the deferral would not be meaningful if, by staying, the alien could be barred from re-entry for three to ten years. To avoid this outcome, the former Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS), now United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), essentially deemed that aliens with such deferrals are “lawfully present” so that they do not accrue days of unlawful presence and are not subject to the statutory bars.[5]

For this study’s purposes, we use the definition that conforms to U.S. immigration law and consider individuals present in the U.S. without legal status to be illegal aliens, regardless of any deferments applicable to their removal or accrual of unlawful presence. Counting individuals in these situations as “legal immigrants” or “lawful residents” would be both incorrect and a biased mischaracterization of immigration law.

FAIR offers additional details on who should be considered an illegal alien in our publication titled “Why ‘Illegal Alien’ is the Correct Term.”[6]



CHALLENGES ESTIMATING THE ILLEGAL ALIEN POPULATION

Estimating the size, distribution, and characteristics of the illegal alien population is an inexact science. We can only estimate these figures based on annual and monthly census data.

Most of the current estimates regarding the total number of illegal aliens are based on U.S. Census Bureau data. Unfortunately, far too many of these tallies presume that essentially all unlawful migrants are willing to respond to demographic questionnaires and that they provide accurate information to federal officials.
